newsitem.title: UK: EU cash sugar under pressure, homes hard to find.
newsitem.headline: EU cash sugar under pressure, homes hard to find.

text.p: Premiums for European Union (EU) white sugars should continue to drift lower due to excess supply and increasing difficulty in placing exports in traditional homes, physical sugar brokers said on Thursday.

Spot EU premiums have fallen recently to around $9 over the December contract after around $12 two weeks ago, with further forward delivery periods such as March quoted at around $5 when more C-quota sugar should be on the market.
"It's looking more bearish by the minute -- the crop is picking up daily. I think we should see it (the EU premium) coming off a little bit more," one broker said.
"A lot of the EU producers are trying to pump it out now, they don't want to put it in their warehouses and are looking to put it on the market," he said.
Although producers were receiving relatively low cash returns due to weak world prices, they were trying to sell now as market sentiment was generally bearish, he added.
Another trader suggested that the declining values for spot cargoes were encouraging many buyers to take sugars on a hand-to-mouth basis and not commit themselves too far ahead.
"Now that the spot premium is disappearing, you'll have a lot more people buying as they need it, rather than buying forward," she said.
Availability is widely thought to be good into 1997 although cargoes needed this year are scarcer as some of the crop has already been sold forward, market sources said.
More producer selling was likely in the first half of next year when trade players bought back short positions which they had taken against sales, they said.

"You may find with the forward months, when May 1997 becomes spot month, that a lot of the end-users have done their pricing ...and it's only then the producers will start selling to trade covering shorts," said a broker.

But the EU is expected to have more difficulty placing its exports this crop year due to the gradual erosion of its Middle East market by the region's new refineries and the absence of large-scale Turkish buying, which supported values last year.
Traders said small EU parcels had been entering the Turkish free zones and were probably destined for Georgia and other nations of the former Soviet Union.
"Russia is another home the EUs don't have, the Gulf has dried up as an EU destination with Savola (Jeddah) coming on and talk of a third refinery due to open," the broker said.
Dubai's refinery is already operating while commercial production should commence at the Jeddah plant in the first quarter of 1997. Oman is also said to be planning a refinery.
"The EUs don't have anywhere to go, they can't stay in the EU and they can't go to Russia, the Middle East -- north Africa is the next best," the broker added.
North Africa has been a consistent buyer from the 1996/97 crop as white sugar trickles into Algeria and Tunisia.

"I think we are going to find difficulty in placing European exports this season...there's the lost opportunity of markets that were there last time, apart from what's going on in the Middle East," said a physical sugar trader.
Increasing the EU's sugar stocks would be another possibility, especially after two years of production declines since the 18.4 million tonnes raw value turned out in 1993/94.
"I don't think the stocks are terribly high. But had you not had two poor crops, by their standards -- two million down from the best -- you'd have a great deal more in stock," he said.
Earlier this week, statistician F.O. Licht said EU sugar producers should bear the brunt of a forecast fall in world imports, couple with added competition from the new refineries.

"Not only is import demand in the developing countries likely to fall...but in Europe, Turkey and ex-Yugoslavia will need much less while the Russian government has taken active steps to deter white sugar imports by raising taxes and duties," Licht said in its first estimate of the 1996/97 world balance.
